disclaimer: Decision support only. Consult a local agronomist before applying any product. Always follow product labels and local regulations.

Pepper___bell_Bacterial_spot.cause: Bacteria Xanthomonas spp. (mainly X. euvesicatoria on pepper)
Pepper___bell_Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small water-soaked leaf spots that darken, sometimes with a yellow halo; infected leaves drop early, exposing fruit to sunscald; small raised scab-like lesions on fruit.
Pepper___bell_Bacterial_spot.chemical_treatment: Fixed copper tank-mixed with mancozeb, applied preventively; products protect healthy tissue but do not cure existing infections (follow the product label).
Pepper___bell_Bacterial_spot.organic_treatment: OMRI-listed copper formulations or Bacillus-based products; combine with strict sanitation and resistant cultivars.
Pepper___bell_Bacterial_spot.immediate_action: Remove and destroy crop debris; do not spray, tie, harvest or handle plants while wet; sanitize stakes, tools and trays.
Pepper___bell_Bacterial_spot.prevention: Use certified pathogen-free seed and disease-free transplants, bacterial spot-resistant pepper cultivars, rotation to non-solanaceous crops, and solanaceous weed control; avoid overhead irrigation and splashing water.
Pepper___bell_Bacterial_spot.severity_guidance: Rapid leaf drop with widespread fruit lesions means sprays can only slow spread, not cure it; focus on protecting healthy plants and on sanitation.
sources: NC State Extension — Bacterial Spot of Pepper and Tomato, https://content.ces.ncsu.edu/bacterial-spot-of-pepper-and-tomato, accessed 2026-10-12

Alabama Cooperative Extension System — Bacterial Spot in Peppers and Tomatoes (E. Sikora, 2020), https://www.aces.edu/blog/topics/crop-production/bacterial-spot-in-peppers-and-tomatoes/, accessed 2026-10-12

Pepper___healthy.cause: No pathogen; plant shows normal growth.
Pepper___healthy.symptoms: Uniform green leaves without spots, wilting, or unusual mottling; fruit develops normally.
Pepper___healthy.organic_treatment: None needed; continue cultural best practices.
Pepper___healthy.immediate_action: Continue routine scouting for early spots, insects, and nutrient stress.
Pepper___healthy.prevention: Balanced fertility, disease-free seed and transplants, control of solanaceous weeds, and avoiding overhead irrigation.
Pepper___healthy.severity_guidance: No disease action required; re-check after weather events that favor foliar disease.
sources: NC State Extension — Bacterial Spot of Pepper and Tomato, https://content.ces.ncsu.edu/bacterial-spot-of-pepper-and-tomato, accessed 2026-10-12

Alabama Cooperative Extension System — Bacterial Spot in Peppers and Tomatoes (E. Sikora, 2020), https://www.aces.edu/blog/topics/crop-production/bacterial-spot-in-peppers-and-tomatoes/, accessed 2026-10-12

Potato___Early_blight.cause: Fungus Alternaria solani (and related Alternaria species)
Potato___Early_blight.symptoms: Dark brown leaf lesions with concentric rings (target-like), often on older leaves; yellowing and premature defoliation.
Potato___Early_blight.chemical_treatment: Protectant fungicides such as chlorothalonil or mancozeb on a regular schedule under disease-favorable weather; alternate FRAC groups (follow the product label).
Potato___Early_blight.organic_treatment: Copper fungicides labeled for potato early blight; improve airflow and reduce leaf wetness.
Potato___Early_blight.immediate_action: Remove heavily blighted lower leaves; avoid overhead irrigation late in the day.
Potato___Early_blight.prevention: Crop rotation, adequate nitrogen (avoid severe stress), certified seed tubers, and hilling/mulch to reduce soil splash.
Potato___Early_blight.severity_guidance: If lesions move into the upper canopy before tuber bulking is complete, intensify protectant sprays and consult local extension timing guidance.
sources: University of Florida IFAS — Potato Early Blight, https://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/PP128, accessed 2026-10-11

Potato___Late_blight.symptoms: Water-soaked spots at leaf tips and edges that turn brown, often with a yellow halo; white moldy growth on lower leaf surfaces in cool, wet weather; reddish-brown rot extending into tubers.
Potato___Late_blight.chemical_treatment: Protectant fungicides (e.g. chlorothalonil, mancozeb) applied before symptoms, alternated with systemic products to limit resistance; time sprays using weather-based forecasts (follow the product label).
Potato___Late_blight.organic_treatment: Copper hydroxide or copper sulfate where permitted for organic crops; needs early, thorough coverage and strict sanitation.
Potato___Late_blight.immediate_action: Spray the whole field as soon as late blight is found; quickly kill infected pockets; destroy cull piles and leftover tubers; kill vines completely before harvest.
Potato___Late_blight.prevention: Plant certified seed, destroy volunteer potatoes and cull piles, choose well-drained sites, plant on ridges and hill well, and monitor regional late-blight forecasts.
Potato___Late_blight.severity_guidance: Rapid spread in cool, wet weather is an emergency: treat the entire field immediately; if more than 5% of tubers are infected, do not store them.
sources: University of Wyoming Cooperative Extension — Potato Late Blight (B-1032, Franc, Brown & Kerr, 1996), https://www.wyoextension.org/agpubs/pubs/B1032.pdf, accessed 2026-10-12
Pacific Pests & Pathogens — Potato late blight (265), https://apps.lucidcentral.org/ppp/text/web_full/entities/potato_late_blight_265.htm, accessed 2026-10-12

Potato___healthy.cause: No pathogen; plant shows normal growth.
Potato___healthy.symptoms: Leaves uniformly green without water-soaked or target-like lesions; stems firm.
Potato___healthy.immediate_action: Keep scouting, especially after cool rainy periods that favor late blight.
Potato___healthy.prevention: Certified seed, rotation, good drainage, and timely hilling.
sources: University of Wyoming Cooperative Extension — Potato Late Blight (B-1032, Franc, Brown & Kerr, 1996), https://www.wyoextension.org/agpubs/pubs/B1032.pdf, accessed 2026-10-12
Pacific Pests & Pathogens — Potato late blight (265), https://apps.lucidcentral.org/ppp/text/web_full/entities/potato_late_blight_265.htm, accessed 2026-10-12

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.cause: Bacteria Xanthomonas spp. (mainly X. perforans on tomato)
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small circular water-soaked leaf spots, sometimes with a faint yellow halo, that turn dark brown to black and can merge into blighted areas; small raised scab-like lesions on fruit.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.chemical_treatment: Fixed copper tank-mixed with mancozeb, starting before symptoms when disease pressure is high; products protect but do not cure (follow the product label).
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.organic_treatment: OMRI-listed copper formulations or Bacillus-based products; emphasize sanitation.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.immediate_action: Do not spray, tie, harvest or handle plants while wet; sanitize tools and stakes; remove crop debris after harvest.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.prevention: Pathogen-free certified seed and disease-free transplants, rotation to non-solanaceous crops, solanaceous weed control, and avoiding overhead irrigation; resistant tomato cultivars are not currently available.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.severity_guidance: Widespread fruit spotting means sprays can only slow spread, not cure it; tighten sanitation and keep protectant sprays within label limits.
sources: NC State Extension — Bacterial Spot of Pepper and Tomato, https://content.ces.ncsu.edu/bacterial-spot-of-pepper-and-tomato, accessed 2026-10-12

Alabama Cooperative Extension System — Bacterial Spot in Peppers and Tomatoes (E. Sikora, 2020), https://www.aces.edu/blog/topics/crop-production/bacterial-spot-in-peppers-and-tomatoes/, accessed 2026-10-12
Clemson HGIC — Tomato Diseases & Disorders, https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/tomato-diseases-disorders/, accessed 2026-10-11

Tomato___Early_blight.cause: Fungus Alternaria solani (now also classified as A. linariae)
Tomato___Early_blight.symptoms: Dark concentric-ringed spots on older leaves, yellowing around spots; can progress up the canopy and affect stems/fruit.
Tomato___Early_blight.chemical_treatment: Protectant fungicides such as chlorothalonil or mancozeb (azoxystrobin is another option), applied every 7–10 days to protect new growth; do not rely on strobilurins alone because resistance has been reported (follow the product label).
Tomato___Early_blight.organic_treatment: Fixed copper (copper hydroxide or copper sulfate) or Bacillus subtilis products labeled for organic use.
Tomato___Early_blight.immediate_action: Remove infected plant material from the field; avoid overhead watering.
Tomato___Early_blight.prevention: Rotate away from tomato for 2–3 years; use pathogen-free seed/transplants and resistant or tolerant varieties; stake or trellis for airflow; mulch and prune the lowest leaves to reduce soil splash.
Tomato___Early_blight.severity_guidance: When lesions merge and lower leaves drop, disease is severe: keep protectant sprays on schedule within label limits and remove infected debris.
sources: Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station — Early Blight of Tomato (Y. Li, 2012), https://portal.ct.gov/-/media/caes/documents/publications/fact_sheets/plant_pathology_and_ecology/earlyblightoftomato032912pdf.pdf, accessed 2026-10-12
NC State Extension — Early Blight of Tomato, https://content.ces.ncsu.edu/early-blight-of-tomato, accessed 2026-10-12

Tomato___Late_blight.symptoms: Large water-soaked grey-green lesions that turn brown/black quickly; white sporulation on leaf undersides in humid weather; firm brown fruit lesions.
Tomato___Late_blight.chemical_treatment: Apply late-blight–labeled fungicides promptly when risk is high; protectants alone may be insufficient under severe pressure (follow the product label and local alerts).
Tomato___Late_blight.organic_treatment: Copper products labeled for late blight plus immediate removal of infected plants; coverage must be thorough.
Tomato___Late_blight.immediate_action: Bag and destroy infected plants (do not compost); notify nearby growers if outbreaks are regional.
Tomato___Late_blight.prevention: Resistant cultivars where available, night-time leaf wetness reduction, and monitoring of late-blight forecast systems.
Tomato___Late_blight.severity_guidance: Any confirmed late blight in humid weather is high severity — act the same day to limit spread.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Late Blight of Tomato, https://extension.umn.edu/diseases/late-blight, accessed 2026-10-11
Penn State Extension — Scouting and Identifying Tomato Diseases, https://extension.psu.edu/scouting-and-identifying-tomato-diseases, accessed 2026-10-11

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.symptoms: Pale yellow spots on upper leaf surfaces with olive-green to brown velvety mold on the corresponding undersides; common in humid greenhouses/high tunnels.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.chemical_treatment: Preventive fungicides labeled for tomato leaf mold (e.g. chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or copper where listed); alternate modes of action (follow the product label).
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.organic_treatment: Copper hydroxide products labeled for leaf mold; improve ventilation aggressively.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.immediate_action: Prune for airflow, reduce humidity, and remove heavily infected leaves.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.prevention: Resistant cultivars, wider spacing, lower night humidity, and avoid wetting foliage.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.severity_guidance: Rapid lower-canopy yellowing with fuzzy undersides in a closed tunnel warrants immediate humidity control plus labeled sprays.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Tomato Leaf Mold, https://extension.umn.edu/disease-management/tomato-leaf-mold, accessed 2026-10-11
Clemson HGIC — Tomato Diseases & Disorders, https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/tomato-diseases-disorders/, accessed 2026-10-11

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.symptoms: Numerous small circular spots with dark borders and tan/grey centers; tiny black pycnidia in lesion centers; defoliation starting from lower leaves.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.chemical_treatment: Protectant fungicides such as chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or copper on a preventive schedule (follow the product label).
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.organic_treatment: Fixed copper fungicides; rely heavily on rotation, mulching, and sanitation because organic efficacy is limited once established.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.immediate_action: Remove infected lower leaves; stake plants; stop overhead irrigation.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.prevention: 2–3 year rotation away from tomato, debris removal, mulch to reduce splash, and weed control of solanaceous weeds.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.severity_guidance: If spots coalesce and lower half of the plant defoliates before fruit ripens, increase spray frequency within label limits and remove the worst foliage.
sources: NC State Extension — Septoria Leaf Spot of Tomato, https://content.ces.ncsu.edu/septoria-leaf-spot-of-tomato, accessed 2026-10-11
Clemson HGIC — Tomato Diseases & Disorders, https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/tomato-diseases-disorders/, accessed 2026-10-11

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.cause: Arachnid pest Tetranychus urticae (not a pathogen)
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.symptoms: Fine stippling on leaves progressing to bronzing; fine webbing on undersides; mites visible with a hand lens.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.chemical_treatment: Use a labeled miticide for twospotted spider mite on tomato; rotate modes of action and do not spray preventively without scouting (follow the product label).
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.organic_treatment: Insecticidal soap, horticultural oil, or neem products labeled for mites; ensure thorough underside coverage.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.immediate_action: Scout leaf undersides; spot-treat hotspots; avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill mite predators.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.prevention: Reduce plant stress and dust; conserve beneficials; quarantine new transplants.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.severity_guidance: Bronzing plus heavy webbing across much of the canopy needs prompt miticide coverage; light stippling can often be managed with spot treatments first.
sources: Michigan State University Extension — Diagnosing Mite Problems in Tomatoes, https://www.canr.msu.edu/news/diagnosing_mite_problems_in_tomatoes, accessed 2026-10-11

Texas A&M AgriLife Extension Entomology — Twospotted Spider Mite Management Guide for Horticulture Crops, https://extensionentomology.tamu.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/twospotted-spider-mite-management-for-horticulture-crops-1.pdf, accessed 2026-10-11

Tomato___Target_Spot.symptoms: Small spots with yellow margins that start on older leaves and move up the plant; larger spots show target-like rings; heavy infection causes yellowing, collapse and leaf drop; stems and fruit can also be affected.
Tomato___Target_Spot.chemical_treatment: Chlorothalonil, mancozeb or copper oxychloride, starting when the first spots appear and repeated every 10–14 days; spray both leaf surfaces and observe the pre-harvest interval (follow the product label).
Tomato___Target_Spot.organic_treatment: Copper fungicides where labeled; remove lower leaves to improve airflow at the base of the plant.
Tomato___Target_Spot.immediate_action: Remove and destroy lower leaves when spots appear.
Tomato___Target_Spot.prevention: Rotate away from tomato for 3 years; collect and destroy crop debris after harvest; remove lower branches for airflow; avoid overhead irrigation; check nursery seedlings for spots.
Tomato___Target_Spot.severity_guidance: When spots spread to all leaflets and leaves yellow and collapse, disease pressure is high: keep sprays on the 10–14 day schedule within label limits.
sources: Pacific Pests & Pathogens — Tomato target spot (163), https://apps.lucidcentral.org/ppp/text/web_full/entities/tomato_target_spot_163.htm, accessed 2026-10-12

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.cause: Begomovirus transmitted by sweetpotato whitefly (Bemisia tabaci)
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.symptoms: Upward leaf curling, yellow leaf margins, stunting, shortened internodes, and reduced fruit set — worse with early infection.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.chemical_treatment: No curative spray for the virus; manage whiteflies with labeled insecticides rotated by mode of action, prioritizing early-season protection (follow the product label).
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.organic_treatment: Insecticidal soaps, oils, or neem products labeled for whiteflies on undersides of leaves; use row covers on young plants where practical.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.immediate_action: Rogue infected plants when incidence is still low; control whiteflies on remaining plants; destroy crop residue after harvest.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.prevention: TYLCV-tolerant cultivars, virus-free transplants, reflective mulch, weed host management, and avoid planting next to old infected fields.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.severity_guidance: Early-season infection with many whiteflies is high impact — replace plants if fruit set has failed and pressure remains high.
sources: NC State Extension — Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus, https://content.ces.ncsu.edu/tomato-yellow-leaf-curl-virus, accessed 2026-10-11
UC IPM — Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl, https://ipm.ucanr.edu/agriculture/tomato/tomato-yellow-leaf-curl/, accessed 2026-10-11

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.cause: Tobamovirus (Tomato mosaic virus / Tobacco mosaic virus complex); spreads mechanically via sap, seed, and contaminated tools
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.symptoms: Mosaic mottling of light and dark green on leaves, leaf distortion, stunting; fruit may show uneven color or deformation.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.chemical_treatment: None needed for the virus itself — no effective curative chemical; focus on sanitation and resistant cultivars.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.organic_treatment: None curative; use hygiene (milk or bleach tool dips as recommended by extension) and resistant varieties.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.immediate_action: Remove and destroy infected plants including roots; do not compost; wash hands and disinfect tools before touching healthy plants.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.prevention: Certified seed, resistant cultivars (TMV/ToMV codes), weed control, and avoid tobacco products when handling plants.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.severity_guidance: Any confirmed mosaic spread in a block is high risk because of mechanical transmission — rogue promptly and sanitize thoroughly.
sources: Utah State University Extension — Tomato and Tobacco Mosaic Virus, https://extension.usu.edu/planthealth/ipm/notes_ag/veg-TMV-ToMV, accessed 2026-10-11
University of Kentucky — Managing Tobamoviruses in Greenhouse Production, https://plantpathology.ca.uky.edu/files/ppfs-gh-08.pdf, accessed 2026-10-11

Tomato___healthy.cause: No pathogen; plant shows normal growth.
Tomato___healthy.symptoms: Even green foliage without spots, mold, mosaic, curling, or stippling; normal flowering and fruit set.
Tomato___healthy.organic_treatment: None needed; continue cultural best practices.
Tomato___healthy.immediate_action: Continue weekly scouting of lower leaves and leaf undersides.
Tomato___healthy.prevention: Good airflow, drip irrigation, rotation, and resistant cultivars matched to local disease pressure.
sources: Clemson HGIC — Tomato Diseases & Disorders, https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/tomato-diseases-disorders/, accessed 2026-10-11

Orange___Haunglongbing(Citrus_greening).cause: Bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus (vectored by Asian citrus psyllid, Diaphorina citri)
Orange___Haunglongbing(Citrus_greening).symptoms: Asymmetric blotchy mottle on leaves, yellow shoots, vein corking, stunted tree growth, and small lopsided bitter fruit that remains green at the stylar end.
Orange___Haunglongbing(Citrus_greening).chemical_treatment: No curative chemical exists for infected trees; chemical management targets vector control using systemic insecticides (e.g., imidacloprid) or foliar sprays (e.g., pyrethroids, organophosphates) during new leaf flush (follow product label).
Orange___Haunglongbing(Citrus_greening).organic_treatment: Insecticidal soaps, horticultural mineral oils, or neem-based sprays targeting psyllid nymphs; introduction of biocontrol parasitoids such as Tamarixia radiata.
Orange___Haunglongbing(Citrus_greening).immediate_action: Scout for psyllid vectors and blotchy mottle; immediately eradicate confirmed infected trees to eliminate inoculum reservoirs for neighboring groves.
Orange___Haunglongbing(Citrus_greening).prevention: Plant only certified disease-free nursery stock; inspect flush growth for psyllid nymphs; establish windbreaks and quarantine zones to prevent vector migration.
Orange___Haunglongbing(Citrus_greening).severity_guidance: Once a tree is systemically symptomatic with extensive dieback, it cannot be cured; remove the tree immediately to protect surrounding orchard blocks.
sources: UC IPM — Citrus: Huanglongbing and Asian Citrus Psyllid, https://ipm.ucanr.edu/agriculture/citrus/asian-citrus-psyllid-and-huanglongbing-disease/, accessed 2026-10-14

Peach___Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small water-soaked angular lesions on leaves that turn purplish-brown and drop out, creating a shot-hole appearance; fruit develops pitted sunken cracks or oozing gum spots.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.chemical_treatment: Preventive applications of fixed copper or oxytetracycline formulations applied starting at bud break through cover sprays; alternate FRAC groups (follow product label; avoid phytotoxic copper rates post-bloom).
Peach___Bacterial_spot.organic_treatment: Low-rate fixed copper formulations applied during dormancy and pre-bloom; copper-tolerant cultivar selection and orchard sanitation.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.immediate_action: Prune dead twigs or cankers in late winter before bloom; avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization that creates overly vigorous succulent shoots.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.prevention: Select bacterial spot-resistant peach cultivars; plant windbreaks on sandy sites to minimize wind-driven sand abrasion; avoid overhead irrigation.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.severity_guidance: Severe defoliation and fruit cracking warrant strict seasonal protectant spray schedules in future seasons; rescue sprays on heavily cracked fruit offer limited benefit.
sources: Oklahoma State Extension — Peach Bacterial Spot, https://extension.okstate.edu/plants/peach-bacterial-spot, accessed 2026-10-10
Penn State Extension — Bacterial Spot of Peach, https://extension.psu.edu/bacterial-spot-of-peach, accessed 2026-10-14

Peach___healthy.cause: No pathogen; tree exhibits normal vegetative vigor and fruit development.
Peach___healthy.symptoms: Vibrant lanceolate green leaves without shot-hole perforations, curling, or gummy fruit lesions.
Peach___healthy.organic_treatment: None needed; maintain standard orchard sanitation and balanced tree nutrition.
Peach___healthy.immediate_action: Continue routine canopy scouting for early bacterial spot, peach leaf curl, or borer entry holes.
Peach___healthy.prevention: Prune during late dormancy for optimal canopy airflow and light penetration; maintain balanced fertility and drip irrigation.
Peach___healthy.severity_guidance: No intervention required; continue monitoring during high-humidity and warm rainy periods.
sources: Penn State Extension — Bacterial Spot of Peach, https://extension.psu.edu/bacterial-spot-of-peach, accessed 2026-10-14

Raspberry___healthy.cause: No pathogen; canes and foliage exhibit normal growth.
Raspberry___healthy.symptoms: Compound green foliage with serrated edges, free of mosaic mottling, powdery mildew, or cane rust lesions.
Raspberry___healthy.organic_treatment: None needed; ensure proper trellis support and weed management.
Raspberry___healthy.immediate_action: Routine weekly scouting of primocanes and floricanes for cane blights, spider mites, or aphid clusters.
Raspberry___healthy.prevention: Plant certified virus-indexed cane stock in well-drained soil; maintain proper row spacing to facilitate air circulation; prune spent floricanes after harvest.
Raspberry___healthy.severity_guidance: No corrective action necessary; inspect regularly after prolonged rain.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Raspberries: Disease Management, https://extension.umn.edu/fruit/growing-raspberries-home-garden, accessed 2026-10-14

Soybean___healthy.cause: No pathogen; trifoliate leaves display healthy vigor and chlorophyll density.
Soybean___healthy.symptoms: Uniform green trifoliate leaves without frog-eye spots, rust pustules, or interveinal chlorosis.
Soybean___healthy.organic_treatment: None needed; maintain balanced soil fertility and weed control.
Soybean___healthy.immediate_action: Continue routine field scouting during reproductive stages (R1-R5) for foliar blights and soybean aphids.
Soybean___healthy.prevention: Rotate crops with non-legumes (e.g., corn); plant certified pathogen-free seeds treated with inoculants; ensure adequate soil drainage.
Soybean___healthy.severity_guidance: No action required; maintain integrated pest management monitoring through pod-fill.
sources: Iowa State University Extension — Soybean Diseases and Management, https://crops.extension.iastate.edu/soybean-diseases, accessed 2026-10-14

Squash___Powdery_mildew.cause: Fungi Podosphaera xanthii (syn. Sphaerotheca fuliginea) and Erysiphe cichoracearum
Squash___Powdery_mildew.symptoms: White talcum-powder-like fungal patches on the upper and lower surfaces of leaves, petioles, and stems; leaves turn yellow, brown, and senesce prematurely.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.chemical_treatment: Fungicides such as myclobutanil, quinoxyfen, or trifloxystrobin applied at first sign of disease; alternate FRAC classes to avoid resistance (follow product label).
Squash___Powdery_mildew.organic_treatment: Potassium bicarbonate, sulfur formulations, or horticultural neem oil applied preventively on both leaf surfaces.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.immediate_action: Prune and dispose of severely infected older crown leaves; avoid handling wet foliage; ensure adequate air movement.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.prevention: Plant powdery mildew-resistant cucurbit varieties; maintain wide row spacing for canopy aeration; avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.severity_guidance: When white powdery colonies cover more than 20% of leaf area across the canopy, fungicide treatments must be initiated promptly to protect photosynthetic capacity and fruit yield.
sources: Cornell Cooperative Extension — Powdery Mildew of Cucurbits, https://vegetablemdonline.ppath.cornell.edu/factsheets/Cucurbits_PM.htm, accessed 2026-10-14
UC IPM — Cucurbits: Powdery Mildew, https://ipm.ucanr.edu/agriculture/cucurbits/powdery-mildew/, accessed 2026-10-14

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.symptoms: Numerous small irregular purple to dark brownish-purple spots on upper leaf surfaces; spots coalesce causing entire leaf blades to look scorched, dried, and curled upward.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.chemical_treatment: Protectant fungicides containing captan, thiram, or pyraclostrobin/boscalid applied in early spring as new growth emerges, especially before bloom (follow product label).
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.organic_treatment: Copper-based fungicides applied during dormancy or early vegetative emergence; prompt removal of diseased runner leaves.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.immediate_action: Mow and destroy infected foliage immediately after post-harvest bed renovation; eradicate dead runner plants.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.prevention: Plant certified disease-free strawberry crowns of resistant varieties; space plants to promote rapid drying; avoid overhead irrigation; renovate beds annually.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.severity_guidance: If more than 25% of the leaf canopy displays scorch symptoms during fruit development, apply protectant fungicides to prevent runner and calyx infection.
sources: NC State Extension — Leaf Scorch of Strawberry, https://content.ces.ncsu.edu/leaf-scorch-of-strawberry, accessed 2026-10-14
University of Illinois Extension — Strawberry Leaf Scorch, https://extension.illinois.edu/plant-diseases/strawberry-leaf-scorch, accessed 2026-10-14

Strawberry___healthy.cause: No pathogen; crowns, stolons, and trifoliate leaves display normal vigorous growth.
Strawberry___healthy.symptoms: Glossy bright green trifoliate leaves without purple scorch spots, powdery mildew, or angular leaf lesions.
Strawberry___healthy.organic_treatment: None needed; maintain proper mulching with clean straw or plastic and proper crown spacing.
Strawberry___healthy.immediate_action: Continue routine scouting for two-spotted spider mites, leaf spot onset, and crown rot symptoms.
Strawberry___healthy.prevention: Use drip irrigation instead of overhead watering; mulch beds to keep fruit and leaves off bare soil; perform post-harvest bed renovation.
Strawberry___healthy.severity_guidance: No treatment required; inspect canopy after extended warm rainy periods.
sources: NC State Extension — Leaf Scorch of Strawberry, https://content.ces.ncsu.edu/leaf-scorch-of-strawberry, accessed 2026-10-14

Apple___Apple_scab.symptoms: Olive-green to velvety dark brown lesions on leaves and fruit, leaf distortion and premature defoliation, corky scabbed lesions on mature apples.
Apple___Apple_scab.chemical_treatment: Protectant fungicides such as captan or mancozeb applied preventively from green tip through petal fall, or systemic DMI/QoI fungicides alternated by FRAC mode of action (follow product label).
Apple___Apple_scab.organic_treatment: Liquid lime sulfur, wettable sulfur, or fixed copper sprays applied during pre-bloom dormant to pink stages; prioritize leaf litter sanitation.
Apple___Apple_scab.immediate_action: Rake, shred, or flail-mow fallen apple leaves in autumn or apply urea spray to accelerate leaf decomposition and exhaust overwintering ascospores.
Apple___Apple_scab.prevention: Plant scab-resistant cultivars (e.g., Liberty, Enterprise, GoldRush); prune canopies annually for rapid airflow and sun drying; space trees properly.
Apple___Apple_scab.severity_guidance: If primary infections exceed 10% foliar coverage during petal fall, maintain tight 7-day spray intervals to protect developing fruitlets.
sources: Cornell Cooperative Extension — Apple Scab (Venturia inaequalis), https://ecommons.cornell.edu/handle/1813/43074, accessed 2026-10-15
Penn State Extension — Apple Scab, https://extension.psu.edu/apple-scab, accessed 2026-10-15

Apple___Black_rot.symptoms: Small purple leaf spots that enlarge into circular lesions with tan centers and dark borders ('frogeye' spot); firm brown concentric rot on fruit with tiny black pycnidia; sunken branch cankers.
Apple___Black_rot.chemical_treatment: Captan, thiophanate-methyl, or strobilurin-based fungicides included in the post-bloom cover spray schedule (follow product label).
Apple___Black_rot.organic_treatment: Copper formulations applied during early season; aggressive sanitation to excise mummified fruit and dead wood.
Apple___Black_rot.immediate_action: Prune out dead shoots, fire blight strikes, and cankered limbs at least 15 cm below infected tissue; remove all mummified fruit from the orchard.
Apple___Black_rot.prevention: Maintain orchard sanitation, prevent mechanical trunk and limb wounds, control fire blight promptly, and ensure balanced tree nutrition to reduce stress.
Apple___Black_rot.severity_guidance: Presence of limb cankers near fruiting spurs indicates high inoculum pressure; excise cankers during winter pruning and apply protectant sprays before warm rain events.
sources: University of Kentucky Extension — Apple Black Rot, https://plantpathology.ca.uky.edu/files/ppfs-fr-t-13.pdf, accessed 2026-10-15
Penn State Extension — Fruit Diseases: Apple Black Rot, https://extension.psu.edu/apple-disease-black-rot, accessed 2026-10-15

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.cause: Fungus Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae (requires Juniperus virginiana alternate host)
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.symptoms: Bright yellow-orange circular leaf lesions that exude orange droplets, later developing raised tubular aecia (cluster cups) on the leaf underside; distorted fruit spots.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.chemical_treatment: Myclobutanil, propiconazole, or mancozeb applied preventively between pink bud and petal fall when cedar galls are gelatinizing (follow product label).
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.organic_treatment: Sulfur or copper sprays applied prior to rainfall events during ascospore dispersal; cultural eradication of nearby galls.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.immediate_action: Inspect surrounding perimeter for eastern red cedar trees and prune out brown galls or gelatinous orange spore horns in early spring.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.prevention: Select rust-resistant apple cultivars; eradicate eastern red cedar and ornamental junipers within 1 to 2 miles of commercial orchards where feasible.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.severity_guidance: Severe foliar infection causing premature leaf drop weakens flower bud development for next year's crop; ensure timely fungicide coverage during rainy spring periods.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Cedar Apple Rust, https://extension.umn.edu/plant-diseases/cedar-apple-rust, accessed 2026-10-15
NC State Extension — Cedar Apple Rust, https://content.ces.ncsu.edu/cedar-apple-rust-1, accessed 2026-10-15

Apple___healthy.cause: No pathogen; tree exhibits normal vegetative development.
Apple___healthy.symptoms: Uniform dark green foliage without spots, necrosis, curling, or powdery sporulation; robust shoot growth and fruit set.
Apple___healthy.organic_treatment: None needed; maintain standard orchard sanitation and balanced tree nutrition.
Apple___healthy.immediate_action: Continue routine scouting for early signs of scab, mites, and codling moth larvae.
Apple___healthy.prevention: Annual dormant pruning to open canopy for sunlight and air drying, balanced fertilization based on soil tests, and proper irrigation management.
Apple___healthy.severity_guidance: No disease action required; maintain routine seasonal pest scouting.
sources: Penn State Extension — Apple Tree Management and Pruning, https://extension.psu.edu/pruning-apple-trees, accessed 2026-10-15

Blueberry___healthy.cause: No pathogen; bush exhibits normal vegetative vigor and berry development.
Blueberry___healthy.symptoms: Glossy green leaves free of necrotic spots, stem cankers, or interveinal chlorosis; firm, clean canes.
Blueberry___healthy.organic_treatment: None needed; maintain pine bark or sawdust mulch and acidic soil conditions.
Blueberry___healthy.immediate_action: Routine monitoring of canes and foliage for blueberry scorch virus, mummy berry, or Japanese beetles.
Blueberry___healthy.prevention: Maintain soil pH between 4.5 and 5.2, ensure consistent drip irrigation, replenish acidic organic mulch annually, and prune old non-productive canes.
Blueberry___healthy.severity_guidance: No disease action required; check leaf tissue nutrients annually.
sources: Michigan State University Extension — Blueberry Growth and Disease Scouting, https://www.canr.msu.edu/blueberries/, accessed 2026-10-15

Cherry___healthy.cause: No pathogen; tree foliage and shoots exhibit normal physiological development.
Cherry___healthy.symptoms: Uniform vibrant green leaves without shot-hole perforations, powdery patches, or bacterial gummosis on twigs.
Cherry___healthy.organic_treatment: None needed; maintain good sanitation and canopy aeration.
Cherry___healthy.immediate_action: Continue weekly scouting for early signs of cherry leaf spot, brown rot blossom blight, or cherry fruit fly.
Cherry___healthy.prevention: Prune canopies to improve airflow and rapid leaf drying, avoid overhead irrigation, and remove wild Prunus species near the orchard border.
Cherry___healthy.severity_guidance: No disease action required; keep regular inspection after humid warm spells.
sources: Pacific Northwest Plant Disease Management Handbook — Cherry (Prunus spp.), https://pnwhandbooks.org/plantdisease/host-disease/cherry-prunus-spp, accessed 2026-10-15

Cherry___Powdery_mildew.symptoms: Circular patches of white powdery fungal mycelium on leaves and green fruit; leaves curl upward and become distorted; fruit develops sunken, deformed blemished patches.
Cherry___Powdery_mildew.chemical_treatment: Demethylation inhibitors (DMI), quinone outside inhibitors (QoI), or succinate dehydrogenase inhibitors (SDHI) applied starting at shuck fall (follow product label).
Cherry___Powdery_mildew.organic_treatment: Wettable sulfur, potassium bicarbonate, or horticultural narrow-range oils applied preventively on expanding tender leaves.
Cherry___Powdery_mildew.immediate_action: Prune out water sprouts and succulent canopy growth that trap moisture and serve as primary infection reservoirs.
Cherry___Powdery_mildew.prevention: Open tree canopies via proper summer and dormant pruning to increase light penetration and air movement; avoid excess nitrogen fertilization.
Cherry___Powdery_mildew.severity_guidance: If powdery colonies appear on green fruit before straw-color stage, intensify fungicide protectant applications immediately to prevent crop loss.
sources: Washington State University Extension — Cherry Powdery Mildew, http://treefruit.wsu.edu/crop-protection/disease-management/cherry-powdery-mildew/, accessed 2026-10-15
UC IPM — Cherry Powdery Mildew, https://ipm.ucanr.edu/agriculture/cherry/powdery-mildew/, accessed 2026-10-15

Corn___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray_leaf_sp.symptoms: Small tan spots with yellow halos that elongate into narrow rectangular lesions strictly bounded by leaf veins; lesions become grayish-brown with fungal sporulation.
Corn___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray_leaf_sp.chemical_treatment: Foliar fungicides combining triazole and strobilurin modes of action (e.g., azoxystrobin + propiconazole) applied between VT (tasseling) and R2 (blister) stages if threshold is reached (follow product label).
Corn___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray_leaf_sp.organic_treatment: Crop residue management, deep tillage in high-debris fields where conservation tillage is not critical, and bio-fungicides applied at early whorl.
Corn___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray_leaf_sp.immediate_action: Scout third leaf below ear leaf at tasseling; if lesions are present on 50% of plants in susceptible hybrids, schedule a fungicide application.
Corn___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray_leaf_sp.prevention: Plant corn hybrids with high genetic tolerance or resistance; rotate with non-host crops (soybeans, small grains) for at least 1-2 years; manage surface crop residue.
Corn___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray_leaf_sp.severity_guidance: Lesions progressing to the ear leaf or above before or during silking lead to significant yield reduction and stalk rot; timely chemical protection is critical.
sources: Purdue Extension — Gray Leaf Spot of Corn, https://www.extension.purdue.edu/extmedia/bp/bp-04-w.pdf, accessed 2026-10-15
Iowa State University Extension — Corn Diseases: Gray Leaf Spot, https://crops.extension.iastate.edu/cropnews/2021/07/gray-leaf-spot-corn, accessed 2026-10-15

Corn___Common_rust.symptoms: Oval to elongate cinnamon-brown powdery pustules (uredinia) scattered across both upper and lower leaf surfaces; pustules rupture the leaf epidermis and turn dark brown to black late in the season.
Corn___Common_rust.chemical_treatment: Triazole, strobilurin, or premix foliar fungicides applied when rust pustules appear on upper leaves before blister stage (follow product label).
Corn___Common_rust.organic_treatment: Sulfur or biological control agents (e.g., Bacillus amyloliquefaciens); rely primarily on planting resistant cultivars.
Corn___Common_rust.immediate_action: Scout sweet corn or seed corn inbreds early; apply fungicides if pustules cover >5% of leaves prior to silking under cool, humid weather.
Corn___Common_rust.prevention: Plant resistant field corn hybrids containing Rp resistance genes; plant early in the season to evade southern spore storm arrivals.
Corn___Common_rust.severity_guidance: Commercial dent corn rarely requires treatment unless infection strikes early on susceptible inbred lines during extended cool humid periods.
sources: University of Illinois Extension — Common Rust of Corn, https://cropwatch.unl.edu/plantdisease/corn/common-rust, accessed 2026-10-15
University of Wisconsin Extension — Corn Rust Diseases, https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/common-rust-of-corn, accessed 2026-10-15

Corn___Northern_Leaf_Blight.symptoms: Large elongated cigar-shaped grayish-green to tan lesions (2.5 to 15 cm long) on leaves; under moist conditions, dark olive-brown spores form inside the lesion centers.
Corn___Northern_Leaf_Blight.chemical_treatment: QoI, DMI, or SDHI fungicides (e.g., pyraclostrobin, fluxapyroxad, or tebuconazole) applied from V12 to R2 if disease reaches the ear leaf (follow product label).
Corn___Northern_Leaf_Blight.organic_treatment: Bio-fungicides applied at early vegetative stages; comprehensive field residue shredding and burial to reduce overwintering conidia.
Corn___Northern_Leaf_Blight.immediate_action: Scout fields before silking; if lesions are detected on leaves beneath the ear on 50% of surveyed plants, treat before full tasseling.
Corn___Northern_Leaf_Blight.prevention: Select corn hybrids with specific Ht resistance genes and multigenic background tolerance; practice 2-year crop rotation; till infected residues.
Corn___Northern_Leaf_Blight.severity_guidance: Extensive blighting of the ear leaf and upper canopy before milk stage (R3) drastically impairs grain fill and promotes premature plant death.
sources: Iowa State University Extension — Northern Corn Leaf Blight, https://crops.extension.iastate.edu/cropnews/2020/07/northern-corn-leaf-blight, accessed 2026-10-15
Purdue Extension — Northern Corn Leaf Blight, https://www.extension.purdue.edu/extmedia/BP/BP-84-W.pdf, accessed 2026-10-15

Corn___healthy.cause: No pathogen; corn displays normal vegetative and reproductive vigor.
Corn___healthy.symptoms: Broad, robust arching green leaves free of chlorotic striping, rust pustules, or elliptical blighted lesions; clean stalk and husk tissue.
Corn___healthy.organic_treatment: None needed; maintain balanced soil nutrition and weed management.
Corn___healthy.immediate_action: Continue weekly scouting during critical reproductive windows (V10 through R3) for foliar disease onset or insect pests.
Corn___healthy.prevention: Soil testing to ensure appropriate nitrogen and potassium balance; optimal planting population and seed depth; weed and insect integrated pest management.
Corn___healthy.severity_guidance: No intervention needed; continue scouting through dent stage.
sources: Purdue Extension — Corn Growth and Development, https://www.agry.purdue.edu/ext/corn/pubs/agry9101.pdf, accessed 2026-10-15

Grape___Black_rot.symptoms: Small circular tan-to-reddish leaf spots surrounded by a dark brown margin with tiny black pycnidia arranged in a ring; berries shrivel into hard, black, wrinkled mummies.
Grape___Black_rot.chemical_treatment: Mancozeb, captan, or myclobutanil applied preventively starting at 1- to 3-inch shoot growth through 4 weeks post-bloom (follow product label).
Grape___Black_rot.organic_treatment: Copper-based fungicides applied early in the season; aggressive winter pruning and destruction of mummified berries from the canopy and ground.
Grape___Black_rot.immediate_action: Remove and destroy all mummified grape clusters and infected canes during dormancy or whenever spotted.
Grape___Black_rot.prevention: Trellis and prune for full sunlight and rapid wind drying of the canopy; eliminate wild riverbank grapes near vineyards; cultivate beneath trellises to bury mummies.
Grape___Black_rot.severity_guidance: Berry infection during bloom to pea-size stage causes total cluster mummification; strict protectant timing around bloom is mandatory.
sources: Ohio State University Extension — Black Rot of Grape, https://ohioline.osu.edu/factsheet/plpath-fru-24, accessed 2026-10-15
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Grape Black Rot, https://grapesandwine.cals.cornell.edu/extension/fact-sheets/, accessed 2026-10-15

Grape___Esca_Black_Measles.cause: Fungal complex including Phaeomoniella chlamydospora, Phaeoacremonium minimum, and Fomitiporia mediterranea
Grape___Esca_Black_Measles.symptoms: Interveinal chlorosis and necrosis creating a characteristic 'tiger-stripe' pattern on leaves; dark purple or black spotting on berries ('measles'); internal wood reveals dark vascular streaking and spongy white heart rot.
Grape___Esca_Black_Measles.chemical_treatment: No curative chemical sprays exist; protect pruning wounds with wound sealants or fungicides containing thiophanate-methyl or pyraclostrobin (follow product label).
Grape___Esca_Black_Measles.organic_treatment: Trichoderma-based biocontrol agents applied directly to fresh pruning wounds to prevent spore colonization; surgical excision of infected cordons.
Grape___Esca_Black_Measles.immediate_action: Flag and map symptomatic vines in late summer; delay pruning until late winter (dormancy end) when wound healing is rapid.
Grape___Esca_Black_Measles.prevention: Avoid large pruning cuts where possible; sanitize pruning shears between vines with alcohol or bleach solution; rogue and burn dead or decaying vines.
Grape___Esca_Black_Measles.severity_guidance: Chronic vine decline reduces yield year over year; sudden collapse ('apoplexy') during hot dry spells is fatal to individual trunks, requiring retraining from ground suckers.
sources: UC IPM — Grape: Esca (Black Measles), https://ipm.ucanr.edu/agriculture/grape/esca-black-measles/, accessed 2026-10-15
Penn State Extension — Grapevine Trunk Diseases, https://extension.psu.edu/grapevine-trunk-diseases, accessed 2026-10-15

Grape___Leaf_blight Isariopsis_Leaf_Spot.symptoms: Irregular reddish-brown to dark necrotic spots on leaves, often coalescing into larger blighted areas; severe premature defoliation of the canopy in late summer.
Grape___Leaf_blight Isariopsis_Leaf_Spot.chemical_treatment: Broad-spectrum protectant fungicides such as copper hydroxide, mancozeb, or strobilurins applied during post-bloom canopy management (follow product label).
Grape___Leaf_blight Isariopsis_Leaf_Spot.organic_treatment: Fixed copper formulations or sulfur sprays applied post-veraison; canopy hedging to maximize airflow.
Grape___Leaf_blight Isariopsis_Leaf_Spot.immediate_action: Prune and dispose of blighted foliage; avoid overhead irrigation; clean vine floor of premature fallen leaf litter.
Grape___Leaf_blight Isariopsis_Leaf_Spot.prevention: Maintain open canopy architecture with shoot thinning, leaf pulling in the fruit zone, and annual dormant pruning; destroy vineyard leaf litter.
Grape___Leaf_blight Isariopsis_Leaf_Spot.severity_guidance: Premature defoliation before harvest prevents adequate sugar accumulation and bud cold-hardiness; post-harvest sprays may be required if defoliation is extensive.
sources: University of Florida IFAS — Grape Leaf Spot and Blight, https://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/MG329, accessed 2026-10-15
Pacific Pests & Pathogens — Grapevine leaf spot (Phaeoisariopsis), https://apps.lucidcentral.org/ppp/text/web_full/entities/grapevine_leaf_spot_412.htm, accessed 2026-10-15

Grape___healthy.cause: No pathogen; vine foliage and clusters demonstrate healthy physiological development.
Grape___healthy.symptoms: Uniform green palmate leaves free of lesions, tiger-striping, or powdery coatings; healthy tendril and cluster formation.
Grape___healthy.organic_treatment: None needed; continue routine trellis maintenance and vineyard weed control.
Grape___healthy.immediate_action: Continue routine scouting for black rot, downy mildew, powdery mildew, and grape berry moth.
Grape___healthy.prevention: Canopy management (leaf removal, shoot positioning), adequate drip irrigation, balanced potassium and nitrogen nutrition, and annual winter pruning.
Grape___healthy.severity_guidance: No disease action required; inspect foliage weekly after rainfall events.
sources: Cornell Cooperative Extension — Grape Canopy Management, https://grapesandwine.cals.cornell.edu/extension/, accessed 2026-10-15
